svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra ID editions, showing four capabilities that cost nothing, the ladder from Free through P1, P2, ID Governance and the Entra Suite with what each rung unlocks, the counting rule that licences are held for everyone in scope rather than everyone who acts, and the opposite ways Conditional Access and Privileged Identity Management behave when a licence lapses
svg.title: Entra editions price identity per user in scope — and Conditional Access and PIM behave in opposite ways when the licence lapses
svg.text: Thirty posts with no price on them. Identity is where the meter starts.
Azure RBAC costs nothing at any scale. Entra charges per user — and counts every user in scope, not every user who acts.
First, the four things in this phase that still cost nothing
Managed identities
there are no licensing requirements — they can be used at no extra cost (posts #35, #36)
Built-in Entra roles
free — it is the custom ones that are billed, which inverts the trade-off from post #20
Verified ID, core
included with any Entra ID subscription, including Free, at no extra cost
Entra Connect
free and included in your Azure subscription — Connect Health, however, requires P1
The ladder, and the one line each rung actually buys you
Free
Included with Microsoft cloud subscriptions such as Azure and Microsoft 365. Security defaults,
self-service password reset, built-in roles, audit and sign-in logs.
P1
Conditional Access.
Plus SSPR with writeback, custom Entra roles, application proxy,
Connect Health, provisioning logs, and administrative unit administrators.
P2
ID Protection, and so risk-based Conditional Access.
Plus PIM, and access reviews and entitlement management as they were in P2.
ID Governance
An add-on, not a rung — it requires P1 or P2 active in the tenant.
Lifecycle Workflows, auto-assignment policies, ML-assisted access certifications.
Entra Suite
Five products: Private Access, Internet Access, ID Governance, ID Protection and Verified ID
premium capabilities. A P1 subscription, or a package that includes one, is required.
And a sentence that should decide a purchase: no new governance features will be added to the P2 SKU.
You are billed for scope, not for use
A policy lets all 2,000 employees request an access package.
150 of them actually request it.
2,000 licences. 1,850 of them for people who never clicked.
An access review of 500 members, 3 owners reviewing
PIM: 42 eligible + 5 approvers + 6 reviewers
Reviewers are counted too. So are the people being reviewed.
So is the administrator who configured it.
And you do not assign them to anyone
Users don’t need to be assigned a Microsoft Entra ID
Governance license, but there needs to be as many licenses
to include all member users in scope of, or who configures,
the Identity Governance features.
So the licence count is a number you must hold, not a
thing you can point at in a user’s profile.
Nothing in the portal stops you widening the scope of a
policy past the number of licences you own.
And when the licence lapses, the two headline features behave in opposite ways
Conditional Access holds the line
Policies aren’t automatically disabled or deleted. They can be
viewed and deleted, but no longer updated — deliberately, so
you can migrate away without a sudden change in security
posture.
PIM does the opposite
Eligible role assignments are removed. Configuration settings
are removed. Ongoing access reviews end.
And active time-bound assignments become active permanent.
Sources: Microsoft Entra licensing, and Microsoft Entra ID Governance licensing fundamentals, on Microsoft Learn.
